title: Learning Where and What to Restore for Composite Image Restoration
claim: Restoring mixed degradations means choosing both where to spend computation spatially and which expert capacity each degradation type needs.
layout: 3 panels, center input flanked by arrows to left spatial map and right trajectory plot
description: The figure has three parts. In the center is a stack of rainy, dim photos of a windmill by a lake, which is the degraded input. A gray arrow points left to a panel titled "where". It shows the same image overlaid with a patch grid shaded by expert level E1 to E4, from light green to dark navy. Flat sky and water get light, simple experts. The windmill and detailed structures get dark, complex ones. Two zoomed insets labeled Flat and Detailed are linked to patches by lines. A color legend sits below. A right arrow leads to a panel titled "what". It is a line chart with decoder blocks on the x-axis and expert levels E1 to E4 on the y-axis, shown as horizontal colored bands. Three curves are drawn: purple Low-light, blue Rain, and a dashed green Low+Rain that blends the other two.
caption: Composite image restoration requires jointly deciding where and what to restore. The degraded input (center) is processed along two complementary axes. Left (where): each spatial patch is routed to one of the capacity-graded experts (e.g. E1 to E4, simple to complex). Flat regions are handled by lightweight experts, while detailed regions activate higher-capacity ones. Right (what): the expert chosen at each decoder block traces a curve across capacity levels; each elemental degradation (Low-light, Rain) follows its own characteristic trajectory, and the composite Low+Rain path (dashed) blends those of its single-degradation constituents.
abstract: Real-world degraded images often contain multiple co-occurring degradation types, making composite image restoration fundamentally different from the single-degradation setting assumed by most existing all-in-one methods. These methods typically apply uniform spatial computation and single-label task conditioning, limiting both spatial adaptivity and explicit modeling of degradation mixtures. We propose CART (Composite-Adaptive Routing and Task Conditioning), a unified framework that jointly decides where to spend computation and what degradation cues should guide restoration: a spatial mixer routes patches to graded-capacity experts by local restoration difficulty, and a channel mixer routes each image through degradation-specific experts, conditioned on the global task feature with multi-hot classification supervision. Empirically, CART achieves state-of-the-art performance for composite degradation restoration on CDD-11 and delivers the best results to date on the conventional 3-task and 5-task all-in-one benchmarks.
